phase1.intro:
You've been calling super(...) since 2.1 — let's actually unpack everything that keyword can do.

Where should we start?

dialogue: `super(...)` [[key:calls the parent's constructor, and it must be the very first statement in the child's constructor]] — no exceptions. If you don't write it yourself, Java quietly inserts a no-argument `super()` for you.
That's fine if the parent HAS a no-arg constructor — but [[warn:if it doesn't, you must call super() explicitly with matching arguments]], or the compiler has nothing to fall back on.

stickyNote.flavor: 1️⃣ must be first, or Java inserts one for you
stickyNote.definition: super(...) must be the first statement in a constructor. If omitted, Java inserts a no-arg super() — which fails if the parent has no no-arg constructor.

dialogue: `super.methodName()` lets a subclass call the parent's version of a method it just overrode. Student's `introduce()` calls `super.introduce()` first, then adds its own lines — [[key:that's extending behavior instead of just replacing it]].
Less common but worth knowing: `super.fieldName` reaches a parent's field directly, useful when a child declares a field with the exact same name.

stickyNote.flavor: ➕ extending a parent's behavior instead of replacing it
stickyNote.definition: super.methodName() calls the parent's version of an overridden method. super.fieldName accesses a parent field directly when names collide.

dialogue: [[term:Constructor chaining]] means every constructor call in Java quietly climbs the whole inheritance tree — Student's constructor calls Person's, and Person's would call Object's if you kept following the chain up.
[[key:Every class in Java ultimately extends Object]], whether you write extends or not.

stickyNote.flavor: ⛓️ every constructor climbs to Object eventually
stickyNote.definition: Each constructor call climbs the inheritance chain up to its parent's constructor, ultimately reaching Object, which every class extends implicitly.

phase1.openingDialogue: super does three things — calls the parent constructor, calls a parent method, or reaches a parent field — and every chain ends at Object. ⛓️

phase2.errorMessage:
Test.java:14: error: constructor Person in class Person cannot be applied to given types;
    Student(String name, int age, String studentId) {
    ^
  required: String,int
  found: no arguments
  reason: actual and formal argument lists differ in length
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Person doesn't have a no-argument constructor]] — it only has one that takes a name and an age. Student's constructor forgot to call `super(name, age)` explicitly, so Java tried to insert its default no-arg `super()` call for you... except that constructor doesn't exist on Person.

[[key:The fix is exactly one line]]: `super(name, age);` as the very first statement inside Student's constructor. Whenever a parent class doesn't offer a no-arg constructor, [[warn:you MUST call super() yourself with the right arguments]] — Java won't guess which ones to use.

phase3.openingDialogue: Super is your connection to the parent class! 🔗

mcq.question:
What happens if a child's constructor doesn't call super(...) explicitly, and the parent has no no-arg constructor?

A) Java skips constructing the parent entirely
B) A compile error, since Java's automatic super() call doesn't match any parent constructor
C) The child object is created with all default field values
D) super() is optional and never required

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create Employee class with:
• Fields: name (String), salary (double)
• Constructor
• Method: work() — prints "[name] is working"

Create Manager subclass with:
• Field: department (String)
• Constructor with super()
• Override work() — prints "[name] is managing the [department] department"
• Also call super.work() in the override

In main, create a Manager and call work().

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: even a class you write with absolutely no 'extends' clause at all is still secretly extending something — java.lang.Object. That's exactly why every object you'll ever create in Java already has toString(), equals(), and hashCode() available, even before you write a single line of inheritance yourself. We'll dig into Object's own methods properly a bit later in this unit.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you climb the chain further~
